drills.name: Stance & motion
drills.alt: Staggered stance with level and circle drills
drills.desc: The staggered athletic stance — knees bent, hips back, head up, hands leading — moved in every direction without crossing the feet. Level lives in the legs: you raise and lower by bending the knees, never the back. Everything in wrestling is launched from and defended in this position, so it must hold up for six hard minutes.
mistakes: Standing tall when tired — the stance dies from fatigue before it dies from ignorance.
Crossing the feet while circling, giving up balance for a full step.
Bending at the waist with the head down, exposing the front headlock.

drills.name: Penetration step
drills.alt: Level change and drive step for shots
drills.desc: The deep step that carries you from stance into an opponent's legs: change levels by bending the knees, drive the lead knee to the mat between their feet, and keep the head up and back flat. Power comes from the trailing leg pushing the hips forward through the target. Drilled solo down the mat, it is the engine of every leg attack.
mistakes: Dropping the head and reaching with the arms instead of stepping in with the legs.
Changing levels by bowing at the waist rather than bending the knees.
Overstepping so far that the trailing leg can't drive through.

drills.name: Hand fighting
drills.desc: The constant battle for inside control — clearing the opponent's ties, snapping their posture, and winning wrist and collar position before shooting. Good hand fighters make contact heavy: every touch either moves the opponent or clears a lane. Shots taken behind won hand fights succeed at triple the rate of naked shots.
mistakes: Slapping at the hands without follow-up attacks — clearing a tie means nothing if you don't use the opening.
Reaching with straight arms so your own wrists get snatched.
Letting the opponent's collar tie sit on your neck without immediately clearing it.

drills.name: Double leg
drills.desc: The highest-percentage takedown in wrestling: a penetration step to both legs, head tight to the outside hip, hands locked behind the knees. The finish is a lift-and-turn or a driving cut across, powered by the legs while the back stays flat. Speed of the level change hides the shot; leg drive finishes it.
mistakes: Shooting from too far out and arriving with no drive left.
Head down and inside, taking the full brunt of the sprawl on the neck.
Stalling on the knees after contact instead of running the feet immediately.

drills.name: Single leg
drills.desc: Attacking one leg and hugging it to your chest with head pressure on the inside or outside. From there the finishes multiply — run the pipe, lift and trip, or dump to the far side — all driven by posture and hip pressure rather than arm strength. Holding a fighting opponent's leg is a grip and core endurance test in itself.
mistakes: Holding the leg low at the ankle with a bent back instead of climbing it to the chest.
Letting the head hang outside with no pressure, inviting the whizzer.
Pausing to think while the opponent hops — finishes are chained, not chosen slowly.

drills.name: Ankle pick
drills.desc: A timing attack: a collar tie drags the opponent's weight over one foot, and the free hand scoops that ankle as it lightens. The pick is finished by driving through the collar tie while the ankle is lifted to the hip. It scores off motion — you create the step you attack.
mistakes: Picking at a planted, weighted ankle instead of one in flight.
Bending only at the waist to reach, putting your head below your hips.
Releasing the collar tie during the pick so the opponent squares back up.

drills.name: Sprawl
drills.desc: The reflexive answer to a shot: feet shoot back, hips drop heavily onto the attacker's head and shoulders, legs flare wide out of reach. The whole movement is one violent hip extension — done a beat late it becomes a takedown against you. Wrestlers drill sprawls until the legs move before the mind does.
mistakes: Sprawling onto the knees instead of the hips and toes.
Leaving the legs square and reachable instead of flaring them back at an angle.
Pushing the head away with the hands instead of dropping chest and hip weight on it.

drills.name: Whizzer
drills.alt: Overhook counter to the single leg
drills.desc: A deep overhook thrown over the attacking arm when the opponent is in on your leg, torquing their shoulder down while you limp-leg or hip into them. The whizzer converts defense into offense — enough torque can throw the attacker straight to their back. Force runs through the lat and hip together, never the arm alone.
mistakes: A shallow overhook at the elbow instead of deep at the shoulder.
Whizzering while square — hips must turn in to generate torque.
Hanging on the whizzer while the opponent switches to a double.

drills.name: Snap down
drills.desc: Snapping the opponent's head and shoulders toward the mat off a collar tie and biceps or wrist control. The snap is a whole-body sit-back through the hips, not an arm pull — timed against their forward pressure it plants their hands on the mat. Every snap either scores a go-behind or drains the opponent's posture.
mistakes: Pulling with the arms while standing tall instead of dropping the hips into the snap.
Snapping without circling, letting the opponent recover square.
Pushing the head down and leaving it there — snap and attack, or snap and re-snap.

drills.name: Front headlock
drills.desc: Controlling a broken-down opponent with one arm wrapping the chin and the other cinching their elbow to your chest. Hips stay back and heavy so they cannot penetrate to your legs, while shucks, spins and cradles open up. It is a position of suffocating pressure — held loosely it is a single leg waiting to happen against you.
mistakes: Letting the trapped elbow slip free, which restores the opponent's posture.
Squatting the hips close enough for the opponent to reach your legs.
Squeezing the neck as an end in itself instead of converting to a go-behind or cradle.

drills.name: Go-behind
drills.alt: Shuck and spin to the back
drills.desc: Converting the front headlock or a stuffed shot into rear control by shucking the head aside and spinning around the opponent's anchor point. The spin stays tight — chest glued to their back, weight heavy — because space is what lets them re-square. Fast feet and heavy chest are the entire technique.
mistakes: Spinning wide with light hips, giving the opponent room to turn with you.
Shucking the head without controlling an arm, so they simply look back up.
Stopping halfway behind instead of finishing to the far hip.

drills.name: Duck under
drills.alt: Level change under the tie to the back
drills.desc: Ducking beneath the opponent's elbow off a collar or inside tie, popping up chest-to-back on the far side. The duck is a knee bend and a step — the head slides under a lifted elbow while your tie pulls them over the top of you. It wins with timing against opponents who post or reach with heavy ties.
mistakes: Ducking by bowing the head instead of dropping the level with the knees.
Ducking into a heavy, clamped elbow rather than a lifted one.
Surfacing too far away instead of glued to the opponent's side and back.

drills.name: Hip toss
drills.alt: Headlock or underhook throw over the hip
drills.desc: Stepping across the opponent's body with an underhook or headlock and launching them over your hip. Your hips must land below and across theirs before the throw — then a violent rotation and leg extension does the lifting. Thrown with arms alone it fails; thrown with hips it ends matches.
mistakes: Throwing with the hips still square or beside the opponent instead of across them.
Bending forward at the waist and muscling with the back.
Losing the underhook mid-throw and landing underneath.

drills.name: Bridging
drills.desc: Arching from the mat onto the crown of the head and the feet so the shoulders never touch — the last line of defense against the pin. Combined with a hip turn, the bridge-and-turn escapes bottom positions and reverses near-falls. Neck strength here is built gradually and carefully over months, never rushed.
mistakes: Bridging on the back of the head instead of rolling to the crown.
Flat feet far from the hips, leaving the bridge low and weak.
Bridging straight up without the hip turn that actually escapes the position.

drills.name: Stand-up escape
drills.desc: From bottom position: explode up and into the opponent, control their locked hands, and turn to face them for the escape. The first motion is a violent inside-leg step and hip lift into their pressure — hesitation lets them chop you back down. Hand control before the turn is what separates one point from a re-ride.
mistakes: Standing straight up and away, making the mat return easy.
Turning to face before clearing the opponent's hands from your waist.
A slow first move — the stand-up scores in the first half-second or not at all.
